messages.content: Imagine you're designing a large-scale chat platform with millions of users interacting concurrently. How would you approach scaling the system to handle high volumes of messages, while ensuring performance and reliability, and what trade-offs would you consider?

I own a FastAPI service handling about 40k requests per minute with async SQLAlchemy sessions and versioned routes. We used JWT auth with refresh-token rotation, per-tenant row-level isolation, structured JSON logging, and kept test coverage above 85 percent. When a slow endpoint surfaced I profiled it with cProfile, found N+1 queries in the list endpoint, switched to selectinload and added an in-process cache — p95 dropped from 900ms to 210ms. I also design OpenAPI contracts first so the frontend can build against the schema before the implementation lands.
I'd like to understand your experience with tech system design. Tell me about a time when you faced a significant challenge in this area. How did you approach it and what was the outcome?

Given a design for 10k users growing to 20M, I would start with the constraints: read versus write ratio, consistency needs, and the single biggest failure mode. Start with one Postgres primary with read replicas, an API layer with rate limiting and idempotent writes, and put a CDN in front of static assets. When the DB becomes the bottleneck, partition by tenant id and move hot paths into Redis or Kafka for async processing. I would not jump to microservices — I would keep the monolith until the team and the failure modes demand splitting, and I would define SLOs and error budgets up front so scaling decisions are measurable.

Eight years of Python, most recently designing an LLM evaluation service that scores candidate answers per competency dimension and reconciles them into a composite score. Each answer is sanitized, evidence is extracted, and scores are normalized to avoid model drift between runs. I profile with cProfile, use dataclasses and pydantic for boundaries, and keep the hot loops out of the event loop. I also maintain a knowledge base pipeline that ingests PDFs, chunks them, embeds them, and stores them in per-department Pinecone namespaces so retrieval stays tenant-isolated.

Walk me through a difficult tech event driven problem you solved recently in your Senior Backend Engineer work. What made it hard, and how did you decide between the options?

I work daily with PostgreSQL. We migrated from sync psycopg2 to asyncpg and introduced alembic revisions reviewed in CI. I debugged a deadlock caused by out-of-order row updates and fixed it by ordering lock acquisition consistently. I also run EXPLAIN ANALYZE before touching an index; one change added a partial index on the active-orders flag and cut a join query from 1.4s to 60ms. I understand connection pooling limits, prepared-statement caching in asyncpg, and why you keep migrations backward compatible for zero-downtime deploys.

How do you approach deploying database schema changes in a high-availability environment, and what considerations do you take into account when deciding between blue-green deployments, rolling updates, or other strategies?

For caching I start from the cache invalidation problem, not the cache itself. On a recent service we had a Redis cache with a 30 second TTL that was serving stale pricing data. I changed the write path to invalidate the key on update and used a short TTL as a safety net, plus read-through with single-flight to avoid stampedes. I benchmarked hit rate before and after: from 78 to 96 percent. For a distributed lock I would use Redis SET NX with a lease, and I know when a cache is the wrong tool — e.g. when consistency matters more than latency.

I treat tests as the safety net that lets us refactor. On my last project I introduced a layered test strategy: unit tests for pure logic, integration tests against a real Postgres in a docker compose, and a small set of end-to-end flows for critical paths. Coverage went from 41 to 88 percent while the suite stayed under four minutes by mocking the slowest external calls. I also set up mutation testing for the scoring module — it caught three assertions that never failed. I review test quality in PRs, not just coverage numbers.
